title: Agatha and the Moonbeam Mint
markdown:
Agatha lived in a cottage snuggled into Mount Craggle. Pine needles, distant goat bells. Days usually quiet: herbs, potions of cinnamon and damp earth, Lentil the stoat warned not to chase cloud-shadows too far. Lentil loved sunbeams and crumbs of cheese. Agatha’s magic was not flashing lights. A hum, and a wobbly stool straightened. A whisper, and stubborn seeds pushed through. She liked things to work properly, not to show off.

One blustery afternoon a crumpled parchment fluttered to her window, not by postman but by a gust that rattled the panes. Village elder’s seal: a smudged berry and teacup. Jumbled, clear enough: Urgent. Parcel for Whispering Summit. Moonrise essential. Festival depends on it. Don’t dawdle. Spectacles slid. The annual Lantern Lighting would be a dim affair without whatever was inside. A trapped-moth fear of letting people down: not fast enough, not ready.

“Well, Lentil, our quiet afternoon has become a mountain dash.” She wrapped a strangely shaped package in soft wool. Surprisingly light. Lentil chattered a question, nose twitching. “An important dash. The Lantern Lighting depends on it.” Sturdy stick, beeswax lantern. Crisp air, wind in grey curls. Familiar goat tracks twisted away from pine into wilder, wind-battered heights. The world grew big and grey, fewer trees, sharper rocks.

The path steepened until even the goats would have asked for a second opinion. Wind tugged her cloak like an impatient child. Mist crept in, damp curious ghosts that erased the next three steps. Lentil, usually sure-footed, skittered; happy chatter became anxious squeaks. A stone turned under Agatha’s boot and she sat down harder than dignity preferred. The knot in her tummy tightened. Doubt: not prepared, not good enough, spectacles already halfway down her nose again. Mist whispered the worries back, hid the path, made silence loud. She wanted the fireplace, Lentil on her lap, a potion that smelled of cinnamon and did not involve moonrise.

A voice from behind a mossy boulder. “Lost? Or admiring the interesting weather with deep thoughts?” Cricket the goblin, eyes like tiny glass, grin that didn’t quite reach his ears, a joke held back. Stubby fingers pointing both ways. “Forward is that way if you’re going that way. Or this way if you’re coming from that way. Depends how you look at it.”

“We’re trying to reach the Whispering Summit before moonrise.”

Grin wider, missing front tooth. “Noble! But not quite legendary. Over the crags for a vital delivery is just practical. Now, a grumpy rock troll for a moonbeam sapphire, or a cross cloud giant—that would be a story.”

Agatha ignored the prick. She was doing her job, not making a legend, and felt rather ordinary. She wanted to sit and wait for easier weather. Lentil shivered beside her.

Then a faint familiar sparkle cut the mist, the sort of gleam Lentil chased when it was a cloud and not a plant. His twitching nose led to a crack barely wider than a hand. Among tough moss: a single perfect sprig of moon-dusted mint, leaves pearly, as if someone had been careless with stardust. Not a troll. Not a sapphire. Exactly what a muffin would need, if muffins were allowed to be particular. She picked it. Mint and moonlight filled the crack. The mountain took a clearing breath; mist parted on Whispering Summit, jagged against a sky brightening by the second. Just in time, which for Agatha always felt like accidentally on purpose.

The parcel was not a sapphire. A recipe for Moonbeam Muffins; the final essential ingredient was moon-dusted mint. The village elder, flour always on her apron, clapped. “We’ll have the most wonderful muffins now.”

Unfolded more closely, the slightly singed parchment showed a forgotten step. “Oh dear. Infuse the batter with the essence of the summit—but it doesn’t say how. And the moon will be too high for the mint to catch the light for long.”

Agatha looked at a narrow dangerous ledge, moonlight gathering on rock. “That’s where it needs to infuse. Direct moonbeams. The recipe implies it.”

The elder wrung floury hands. “So narrow. The wind. No one could get there safely.”

Agatha’s heart jumped: heights, tricky places, Lentil hurt. “I can’t go on that ledge.” Knees weak. The drop was a fact, not a story Cricket could improve. If Lentil followed and slipped. She looked at him. He watched the ledge with wide curious eyes, whiskers interested, not afraid. He could go: small, nimble, a thief of sunbeams who had never stolen a fall. He disliked heights; he clung to her sleeve on higher paths and made a noise she translated as absolutely not. Cold dew of hesitation. Wild thyme from below, sharp tang of approaching moonlight. The elder’s floury worry. Children’s disappointed faces if the muffins came out ordinary. Then Lentil’s surprisingly steady gaze, and trust stronger than fear, bubbling up like a potion that had decided to behave.

“Lentil. I need your help. Very special, very brave.” She held out the sprig. “The very edge, where the moonlight is brightest. A moment. Then scamper back.”

He chattered, worry and understanding. Mint in his mouth, paws on rough rock. He edged out, moonlight on sleek fur, wind trying to push him into a story Cricket would enjoy too much. Agatha held her breath, wanted to yell him back, stayed quiet, hands clenched on the walking stick until the wood remembered her fingerprints. A delicate almost-dance: mint dangling in the moon’s first real beam. Shimmering dust from the leaves, a brief constellation no one would catalogue. He scurried back, job done, and shook himself as if the ledge were a puddle. The sacrifice was not a thing. It was his trust, and her decision to let him.

Moon bright, long dramatic shadows across the mountain. Agatha, Lentil, and a surprisingly helpful Cricket (busy collecting lichen he insisted was star-dust and cloud fluff, and which would, he promised, improve any muffin if anyone asked, which no one did) began the descent. Recipe complete. Essence captured. The way down felt lighter, as if the mist had spent its jokes. Lentil trotted, no longer nervous, pausing only to check that Agatha was still attached to her stick. Agatha’s mind held a job well done, not a legend, and the particular warmth of a stoat who had gone where she could not.

Village lanterns bobbed in the evening breeze, a harbour of light in a place with no sea. Moonbeam Muffins: light, fluffy, a taste of moonlight and the ledge, just as the recipe had meant when it was in a hurry. Children giggled and munched; flour appeared on more aprons than the elder’s. Cricket circulated a rumour involving a troll and was politely ignored in favour of second helpings. Later, Agatha’s fireplace, Lentil asleep on her lap, snores a comforting rumble. Steam from a teacup caught firelight, reminded her of mist and the drop. The familiar flutter did not arrive. She scratched behind his ears. Cricket would still want a troll in the story. The muffins did not need one.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
